investigacion.base:
Real-time trackers put Q3 2026 growth at about 3.1–3.6% annualized. The release is still scheduled for October 29, so nothing has resolved yet.

**Resolution sources and schedule**
- **BEA schedule page (snapshot about 34 days old):** It lists the October 29, 8:30 AM release: GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026. BEA's 2026 release calendar matches. I found no sign it has been moved.
- **Delay risk:** There's a precedent. The first three releases of 2026, covering Q4 2025, were rescheduled because the October–November 2025 federal shutdown delayed source data; the advance estimate moved from January 29 to February 20. I didn't search for current shutdown news, so check that.
- **BEA homepage and the Metaculus "credible sources" definition:** I didn't retrieve either page directly.

**Atlanta Fed GDPNow nowcast**
- **Trend:** 3.7% on Oct 1 and Oct 6, then 3.6% on Oct 8. It was 3.6 percent on October 15, unchanged from October 8 after rounding. The unrounded value on FRED is 3.6429.
- **Latest update (Oct 15):** After the retail sales report, the nowcast for real consumer spending (PCE) rose from 3.4 to 3.6 percent. A lower inventory contribution, down from 1.96 to 1.87 percentage points, partly offset this.
- **Composition risk:** Net exports subtract about 2.7 points (-2.69) and inventories add about 1.9 points. Inventories and trade are the most volatile parts of the advance estimate.
- **Next updates:** Oct 20, then probably one or two more before Oct 28.
- **Track record:** A dashboard site says that in the 18 quarters since 2011 whose final nowcast read this high, GDP came in at 3% or more in 11 and above 1% in 16. My own recollection, not checked here, is that GDPNow's historical error against the advance estimate is roughly 1.2 points.

**Other forecasts (as of Oct 19)**
- **Wall Street tracking:** The average Q3 estimate rose to +3.25% from +3.15% the prior week, and the median moved to +3.30% from +3.10%.
- **Morgan Stanley:** Its tracking estimate rose 0.4 percentage point to 3.2% because annual retail sales revisions lifted its consumer spending estimate.
- **Retail sales caveat:** September headline retail sales were strong, but control group sales, which feed into GDP, rose only 0.14%.
- **Trading Economics:** Its own forecast is 3.1%.
- **Prediction markets:** I didn't find any Kalshi or Polymarket prices.

**Recent quarters (current vintages)**
- **Q2 2026:** 1.5 in the advance and second estimates, revised to 2.2 in the third (Sept 30).
- **Q1 2026:** Revised to 2.5% from 2.1%.
- **Q4 2025:** The advance estimate was 1.4%.
- **Q3 2025:** About 3.9–4.4%; sources differ.
- **Inflation backdrop:** Q2 PCE inflation was 5.0%. A high price deflator makes the inflation-adjusted (real) figure more sensitive to how prices are measured.

**Before the release:** The advance September trade and inventory reports, usually out about Oct 27–28, often move the nowcasts a lot. The Q3 GDP release on Oct 29 comes out together with September PCE.

**Bottom line:** Today the central estimate is around 3.1–3.6%. GDPNow is at the high end, and bank trackers are about 3.2–3.3%.

**Sources:**
- [1](https://www.bea.gov/news/schedule)
- [2](https://www.financecalendar.com/us-gdp-report/)
- [3](https://investinglive.com/central-banks/atlanta-fed-gdpnow-holds-at-3-6-for-q3-as-consumer-spending-outlook-improves/)
- [4](https://fedpolicy.org/releases/2026-10-06/gdpnow-2026-q3-oct-6/)
- [5](https://usmacro.com/indicator/gdpnow)
- [6](https://pro.thestreet.com/market-commentary/the-week-ahead-the-rotation-continues)
- [7](https://verifiedinvesting.com/blogs/us-economic-metrics/gdp-q2-2026-third-estimate)

criterios: This question resolves to the percent change in real gross domestic product (GDP) at a seasonally adjusted annual rate for the third quarter of 2026, as stated in the "GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026" news release published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) on October 29, 2026. The figure is the headline "Real GDP" percent change (SAAR) reported in that release (available via the BEA release schedule at https://www.bea.gov/news/schedule and linked from https://www.bea.gov/ ). For example, a reported increase of 2.8 percent resolves as 2.8, and a decrease of 0.5 percent resolves as -0.5.
letra_pequena: Resolution uses the advance (first) estimate only; subsequent second and third estimates do not affect resolution. If BEA reschedules the advance estimate release to a later date (e.g., due to a government shutdown or administrative delay), resolution waits for that release and uses the first published advance estimate of Q3 2026 real GDP growth. If the BEA page is unavailable, the figure as reported by [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) citing the BEA release will be used.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time remaining:** Ten days until the scheduled October 29 release.  
(b) **If nothing changed:** Current tracking estimates point to an advance estimate near 3.2–3.3%.  
(c) **If the current trend continued:** Growth would likely remain around 3.2–3.6%, though the remaining trade and inventory data could move it.  
(d) **Experts and markets:** Recent Wall Street trackers center near 3.3%, GDPNow is 3.6%, and the earlier professional-forecaster median was 2.5%.  
(e) **Low surprise:** Weaker-than-expected trade or inventory figures could pull the advance estimate well below current trackers.  
(f) **High surprise:** Stronger spending or a larger inventory contribution could push it above 4%.

Percentile 10: 1.8%
Percentile 20: 2.3%
Percentile 40: 2.9%
Percentile 60: 3.5%
Percentile 80: 4.0%
Percentile 90: 4.5%

**(a) Time left:** The advance estimate comes out in 10 days, on October 29, 2026. The release is still on BEA's schedule. Shutdown news was not checked, so a small delay risk remains.

**(b) If nothing changed:** GDPNow stands at 3.6% (3.64 unrounded). Bank trackers cluster at 3.2–3.3%, so the outcome would be about 3.3–3.6%.

**(c) If the current trend continued:** Trends point slightly in both directions:
- GDPNow has drifted down slightly (3.7 to 3.6).
- Wall Street trackers have drifted up (3.10 to 3.30 median).

Convergence around 3.2–3.4% looks most likely.

**(d) Experts and markets:**
- Wall Street tracking: average 3.25%, median 3.3%.
- Morgan Stanley: 3.2%.
- Trading Economics: 3.1%.
- Survey of Professional Forecasters (older): 2.5%.
- GDPNow: 3.6%, though it tends to run a bit high.

My central estimate is about 3.2%.

**(e) Low scenario:** The September advance trade and inventory reports (Oct 27–28) could show a much larger inventory drawdown, or less inventory accumulation than assumed (currently +1.9 points). That could knock 1 to 2 points off growth. Weak September consumer spending (control group was only +0.14%) and a high price deflator could push the print to 1.5–2%.

**(f) High scenario:** Imports could fall sharply while inventories hold up, and consumer spending could be stronger after the annual revisions. That could take the print to 4.5% or more.

GDPNow's error against the advance estimate at this horizon is about 1 to 1.2 points. Large offsetting inventory and trade components add to that uncertainty, so I keep the 10–90 range wide.

(a) The time left until the outcome to the question is known: 10 days (scheduled for release on October 29, 2026, at 8:30 AM ET).
(b) The outcome if nothing changed: Approximately 3.2% to 3.3%, reflecting the current consensus of Wall Street tracking estimates.
(c) The outcome if the current trend continued: Around 3.3% to 3.5%, reflecting the recent upward drift in nowcasts following firm headline retail sales data.
(d) The expectations of experts and markets: Atlanta Fed GDPNow sits at 3.6%, Wall Street median tracking estimate is around 3.30% (average 3.25%), Morgan Stanley tracks at 3.2%, and Trading Economics forecasts 3.1%, while earlier survey medians (Philadelphia Fed SPF) were at 2.5%.
(e) An unexpected scenario that results in a low outcome: The projected positive contribution from inventory investment (+1.9 pp in nowcasts) unwinds or net export drag (-2.7 pp) widens further upon arrival of advance September trade/inventory data; a high price deflator erodes real consumer spending gains, driving the advance print down below 1.5%.
(f) An unexpected scenario that results in a high outcome: Inventories accumulate at a faster pace, goods exports surprise to the upside, and real consumer services consumption shows sustained resilience, pushing the print above 4.2%.
